This document explains the structure of a commons project and how to get
started.

```r
library(commons)
```

## Design philosophy

AI agents for data analysis can range from overly cautious, but narrowly
correct, to wildly untrustworthy. Commons is intended to create agents that
produce correct answers by leveraging existing trusted code, while still
allowing the agent enough flexibility to answer novel, realistic questions.
Commons distinguishes between different trust levels based on the analysis
path chosen by the agent.

A core idea behind commons is that, if you are a data analyst, data scientist,
statistical programmer, or other data practitioner, you or your team likely
has a collection of "trusted" code. This is code that you depend on for your
analyses and is used to create apps, reports, and packages. Commons allows you
to take advantage of this code base by encoding it as trusted calculations.

The high-trust "happy path" for the commons agent occurs when the user asks a
question that has a corresponding trusted calculation. In this scenario, the
agent runs that code to get the result. For example, in the biodiversity
example app, if you ask:

> How many total animals were observed at Oak Bluff?

the agent identifies that there exists trusted code that can answer the
question. It runs that code and then reports the results along with a
"Verified answer" tag.

::: {.commons-answer}
> At Oak Bluff, 59 individual animals were observed across 5 species, based on
> 28 hours of survey effort. Note this reflects observed individuals during
> surveys, not necessarily a full census of every animal present at the site.
>
> `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("A")`
:::

Although the agent had to decide which piece of trusted code to run and when,
it did not have to decide _what code to write_, reducing degrees of freedom and
allowing the agent to take advantage of pre-vetted code.

However, we expect most users of agents to also ask questions that stray from
the "happy path." For those, the agent uses additional information to write
custom code. We'll explain the various
[information layers](#information-layers) and the details of the
[trust flow](#trust-flow) in more detail later in this vignette.

## Data sources

One of the primary decisions you'll need to make when building a commons agent
is which data sources to grant the agent access to.

Data sources are supplied to the commons agent with `data_source()`.
`data_source()` takes three arguments: the data, the set of tables to expose,
and the corresponding [data dictionary](#data-dictionaries).

You can supply `data_source()` with an existing DBI connection, named data
frames, or pins. Data frames and pins will be loaded into a DuckDB database.
Database connections will be queried directly.

## Information layers

Commons distinguishes between two primary layers of information: the
_semantic_ layer and the _context_ layer. The semantic layer encodes trusted
code, ideally lifted from verified code that you already use. In a project,
measures are stored in `.R` files; `semantic_layer()` can also accept
`measure()` objects directly. The _context_ layer contains everything else,
stored in Markdown files. Data dictionaries span the two layers. Their
descriptive fields provide context, while
[`definitions`](#definitions) are part of the semantic layer. See
[Data dictionaries](#data-dictionaries) for more information.

| Layer | Sources | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Semantic layer | Measures in `.R` files, [`definitions`](#definitions) in `data-dict.yaml`, and supported [warehouse semantic models](#warehouse-semantic-layers) | Provides trusted calculations. |
| Context layer | Markdown files and descriptive fields in [`data-dict.yaml`](#data-dictionaries) | Informs custom SQL or R and guides interpretation. |

A data dictionary spans both layers: its descriptive fields provide context,
while its governed definitions participate in the semantic layer.

Here are brief examples of a data dictionary, measures `.R` file, and context
layer Markdown file for the biodiversity example app:

::: {.commons-layer-sources .column-screen-inset}
::: {.commons-layer-examples}
::: {.commons-layer-example}

#### Data dictionary

Data dictionaries supply information to _both_ the semantic and context layer.

`dictionaries/warehouse.yaml`

```yaml
tables:
  - name: observations
    description: Species observations by nature preserve.
    columns:
      - name: count
        description: Individuals observed during surveys.
```

:::
::: {.commons-layer-example}
#### Semantic layer

`measures/biodiversity.R`

```r
#' Individuals observed
#'
#' @param site `string` Site name.
#' @measure
individuals_observed <- function(site) {
  sum(observations$count[
    observations$site == site
  ])
}
```

:::
::: {.commons-layer-example}

#### Context layer

`context/biodiversity.md`

```markdown
# Interpreting survey results

Observed individuals reflect organisms
recorded during surveys. They should not
be interpreted as a complete population
census of a nature preserve.
```

:::
:::

:::

## Trust flow

Commons agents will use trusted calculations whenever possible. When the user
asks a question, the agent first searches the semantic layer for a trusted
calculation. If it finds one, it then calls that calculation and the resulting
answer is tagged with a green verified answer pill.

If a relevant trusted calculation is not found, the agent proceeds down the
lower trust path. It searches through the context for additional information,
then uses that information to write custom SQL or R code to answer the user's
question. These answers are either given a citation in a footnote or tagged as
untrusted.

<figure class="commons-flow commons-flow-trusted-calculations column-page">

</div>
<div class="commons-branch-connectors" aria-hidden="true">

<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&searr;</span>
</div>
<div class="commons-branch-routes">
<div class="commons-trust-segment commons-trust-segment-high">
<div class="commons-trust-label">High trust</div>
<div class="commons-trust-steps">
<span class="commons-flow-node">Relevant calculation<br>found</span>
<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&rarr;</span>
<span class="commons-flow-node">Run trusted<br>calculation</span>
<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&rarr;</span>
`r commons:::commons_answer_pill("A")`
</div>
</div>
<div class="commons-trust-segment commons-trust-segment-lower">
<div class="commons-trust-label">Lower trust</div>
<div class="commons-trust-steps">
<span class="commons-flow-node">No relevant<br>calculation found</span>
<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&rarr;</span>
<span class="commons-flow-node">Search context</span>
<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&rarr;</span>
<span class="commons-flow-node">Write SQL/R</span>
<span class="commons-flow-arrow">&rarr;</span>
<span class="commons-flow-results">
<span class="commons-flow-answer">Cited answer<sup class="commons-citation-ref">1</sup></span>
<span class="commons-flow-or">or</span>
`r commons:::commons_answer_pill("C")`
</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
</figure>

There are two possible trust outcomes for the "lower trust" path. When the
agent writes custom SQL or R, it can also include a citation (from a data
dictionary or context layer Markdown file) that supports its approach. Commons
checks that its citation appears as cited in a trusted source. If at least one
citation can be verified, it is displayed as a numbered footnote. If the agent
does not include a citation, or if commons can't verify any of its citations,
the answer gets tagged as `Untrusted`.

The following table details the various ways each trust outcome can occur.

| How the answer is produced | Outcome |
|---|---|
| A trusted R measure | `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("A")` |
| A data-dictionary metric, possibly grouped or restricted using filter or derived-value definitions, or documented columns | `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("A")` |
| A Snowflake semantic-view or Databricks metric-view metric | `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("A")` |
| Custom SQL, including SQL that uses data-dictionary definitions | Cited or `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("C")` |
| Custom R | Cited or `r commons:::commons_answer_pill("C")` |
| No calculation because the available information is insufficient | No label |

## Data dictionaries

You can attach a data dictionary to a `data_source()`. Dictionaries follow the
[`data-dict.yaml` specification](https://data-dict.tidyverse.org/) and provide
structured, source-specific documentation.

```r
warehouse <- data_source(
  con,
  dictionary = "dictionaries/warehouse.yaml"
)
```

Commons agents use data dictionaries in a few ways:

* Dataset-level descriptions and details provide broad, always-available
  context. Glossary terms are included in the system prompt as space allows.
* The first time the agent needs a documented table, it receives the table's
  description, column information, relationships, and relevant glossary terms
  from the dictionary.
* Dictionary prose is available through context search.
* Relationships can guide the agent's join code.

### Definitions

As described in [Information layers](#information-layers), data dictionaries
span the semantic and context layers. Table-level `definitions` are part of the
semantic layer. Each definition is an expression written in
[data-dict's expression language](https://data-dict.tidyverse.org/expressions.html),
not in your database's SQL dialect:

```yaml
tables:
  - name: observations
    columns:
      - name: count
        type: number
    definitions:
      - name: total_individuals
        label: Total individuals observed
        description: Sum of the individuals recorded in surveys.
        expr: SUM(count)
```

#### How commons uses definitions

There are three kinds of definitions. Definitions can participate in trusted
metric calculations or be used in custom SQL.

| Kind | Example | How `call_metrics()` uses it | How custom SQL uses it |
|---|---|---|---|
| Metric | `SUM(n)` | Computes directly | Inserts the expression in `SELECT` or another suitable clause |
| Filter | `status = 'active'` | Filters rows. Can also be a grouping dimension | Inserts a Boolean expression, commonly in `WHERE` |
| Derived value | `price * quantity` | Groups a metric | Inserts a row-level expression, commonly in `SELECT` or `GROUP BY` |

The kind is inferred, not declared. Aggregate and constant expressions are
categorized as metrics, row-level Boolean expressions as filters, and other
row-level expressions as derived values.

See the
[DevRel Agent `data-dict.yaml`](https://github.com/posit-dev/devrel-agent/blob/main/dictionaries/devrel.data-dict.yaml)
for examples of definitions.

When a data source is constructed, commons checks each definition and
translates it to the source's SQL dialect.

## Warehouse semantic layers

If you have trusted metrics in
[Snowflake semantic views](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/views-semantic/overview)
or
[Databricks metric views](https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/uc-semantics/metric-views),
you can use those calculations directly with commons. It can also group or
filter metrics by approved fields from the warehouse, such as region, product,
or date. Answers based on these warehouse-defined metrics are marked as
verified.

## Project directory organization

A commons agent is easiest to maintain when the pieces live in separate files:

```text
.
|-- app.R
|-- agent.R
|-- DESCRIPTION
|-- AGENTS.md # or your coding agent's equivalent (e.g., CLAUDE.md)
|-- instructions.md
|-- dictionaries/
|   `-- warehouse.yaml
|-- measures/
|   `-- sales-dashboard.R
`-- context/
    `-- sales-dashboard.md
```

## Installing the agent skill

The package includes a `commons` [agent skill](https://agentskills.io/) that
helps coding agents build, evaluate, and improve commons agents. We recommend
working with a coding agent that has access to this skill, especially when
building a commons agent. There is a host of useful information contained in
the skill and we assume this is the way most people will work with commons.
That said, the skill and references are also readily understandable to human
readers as well, and you are welcome to ingest the information that way too.

Installing the R package makes the skill files available, but does not
automatically add them to an assistant's skill discovery directory.

Locate the bundled skill with:

```r
skill <- system.file("skills", "commons", package = "commons")
skill
```

### Codex and Posit Assistant

Both [Codex](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills) and
[Posit Assistant](https://assistant.posit.co/docs/reference/config-file#skills)
discover project skills in `.agents/skills`:

```r
dir.create(".agents/skills", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(skill, ".agents/skills", recursive = TRUE)
```

This creates `.agents/skills/commons/SKILL.md`. Commit that directory when the
skill should be available to everyone working in the project.

For a user-wide installation, copy the directory to `~/.agents/skills`. Posit
Assistant also searches `~/.posit/assistant/skills` and
`.posit/assistant/skills` by default. Its `skills.paths` configuration controls
the complete search path; a project-level value replaces, rather than extends,
the global value.

### Claude Code

[Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills) uses `.claude/skills` for
project skills:

```r
dir.create(".claude/skills", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
file.copy(skill, ".claude/skills", recursive = TRUE)
```

This creates `.claude/skills/commons/SKILL.md`. Use
`~/.claude/skills/commons` instead for a personal installation available across
local projects.
